source: Simon (1995) What is a systematic method of scientific discovery? (AAAI Spring Symposium)
finding: Simon, a BACON co-author, states what BACON and human subjects achieved. BACON re-created a dozen or more significant discoveries from the same data the original scientist had. College students rediscovered Kepler's third law at a low rate.
numbers: BACON: 'a dozen or more discoveries' (Kepler to Cannizzaro). Human subjects: Kepler's third law found by 4 of 14 college students (Qin and Simon).
quote: rediscovery of Kepler's Third Law by four of fourteen college students
limits: Secondary summary by the system's own author, not the original 1987 book or 1990 paper. It resolves the '4 of 14' question for gap 3 but is still self-reported.
agent_relevance: A search over simple data transformations is enough to find a law when the data is clean and the variables are pre-chosen. Humans fail most of the time on the same task, so a running check is worth having.

source: Langley, Zytkow, Simon, Bradshaw (1984) The Search for Regularity: Four Aspects of Scientific Discovery (CMU tech report)
finding: Original-source description of BACON.6 search over numeric laws. It scores each candidate parameter set by correlation with the data, uses data only to test and not to generate hypotheses, and so does the same amount of search at any noise level. It always returns some law, or several tied laws when data are very noisy.
numbers: Search starts from parameter values 1, 0, -1; beam of N best states, stops when no state improves. No law counts or noise percentages in this report (OCR text partly garbled).
quote: it is robust with respect to numerical noise
limits: Claims about noise robustness are design claims, not measured rates. Law counts (Boyle, Kepler, Ohm, Coulomb, Snell, Black, Joule) come only from secondary sources seen this session. The 1987 book was not opened.
agent_relevance: A generate-and-test loop where the data only tests is robust to noise by design. Pairs with our rule that a hypothesis must face a check that it cannot influence.

source: Qin and Simon (1990) Laboratory replication of scientific discovery processes, Cognitive Science 14(2)
finding: Fourteen subjects were recorded while trying to find a law for planetary distance and period data. Their search heuristics resembled BACON's. Accounts of how many found the law conflict: the abstract snippet seen says some subjects found it, while Simon (1995) says 4 of 14.
numbers: N = 14 subjects; Kepler's third law (period varies as distance to the 3/2) was the target. Success count: 4 of 14 per Simon 1995 (d01); abstract-level claim unverified.
limits: Not opened: only a search snippet and the catalogue record. Treat the count as 4 of 14 from d01, not from this paper.
agent_relevance: Humans doing discovery use the same heuristics as BACON (try ratios and products of variables). It supports using such transformations as a cheap check step.

source: Liu, Dong, Gao, Feng, Pang (2025) Augmenting research ideation with data: an empirical investigation in social science
finding: Giving the idea generator dataset metadata raised feasibility and expected effectiveness in blind expert pairwise judgments. Novelty dropped slightly. Domain is social science (climate negotiation), not NLP.
numbers: 50 idea pairs (5 ideas per topic x 10 topics), at least 2 annotators each. Metadata: feasibility +20%, expected effectiveness +18%, overall +1.5%, novelty modest decrease. Abstract also states 20% for feasibility.
limits: Small human sample. Generator GPT-Researcher with GPT-4o. Gains are in win-rate percentage points between conditions, not rubric points.
agent_relevance: Grounding ideas in what data exist before generation buys feasibility at some cost in novelty. A cheap grounding step trades novelty for feasibility, which matches the Si ideation-execution gap.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Augmenting research ideation with data: validation before ranking (Table 4)
finding: Gap 1 test. LLM judges ranked a real published idea against LLM ideas. Adding an automatic data-based validation (code interpreter run on the dataset) to the judge input raised ranking accuracy for both judges, mostly on feasibility and effectiveness. Novelty and significance judgments barely moved or fell.
numbers: Ranking accuracy averaged over 4 criteria, 8 papers x 10 LLM ideas, each pair judged twice with positions swapped. Gemini-1.5-Pro 56.9 to 62.3. Claude-3.5-Sonnet 69.0 to 78.9. Feasibility: Claude 20.1 to 46.9, Gemini 29.7 to 55.6. Novelty: Claude 82.5 to 86.9, Gemini 71.3 to 65.8.
limits: Only 8 source papers. Ground truth is that the published idea is the better one, a weak proxy. Token cost of validation not reported. Validation is preliminary, not full experiments.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a cheap executed check changes the judge's accuracy. Judge accuracy above 60% is reachable (Claude 78.9) when the judge sees a computed result, answering gap 5 in part. Cost at equal tokens still untested.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Augmenting research ideation with data: human check of validated selection (Table 5)
finding: Humans compared the top 5 ideas picked by Claude-3.5-Sonnet with and without validation summaries. Validation helped on feasibility and expected effectiveness, not overall.
numbers: Win / tie / loss for with-validation: feasibility 40.0 / 33.3 / 26.7 (p=0.03). Expected effectiveness 43.3 / 27.5 / 29.2 (p=0.02). Novelty 45.0 / 21.7 / 33.3 (p=0.06). Overall 42.5 / 21.7 / 35.8 (p=0.29). Abstract rounds overall gain to 7%.
limits: Z-tests on small counts. The headline '7% better overall' is not significant (p=0.29). Do not cite it as a solid gain.
agent_relevance: Pre-ranking validation moves the dimensions it can measure, and leaves the overall result unproven. Report per-axis, not one pooled score.

source: Si et al. (2026) Towards execution-grounded automated AI research
finding: An automated executor implements LLM ideas as code and runs GPU jobs. A large share of ideas execute. Best-of-50 beats the baseline, and evolutionary search over ten epochs finds clearly better methods. This is execution feedback inside the loop, at real compute cost.
numbers: Execution rate depends on ideator and executor: 42% to 78% when models differ, e.g. 84% vs 42% (GRPO) and 90% vs 78% (nanoGPT) with GPT-5 as executor. Best-of-50 on GRPO: Claude-4.5-Sonnet 60.4% vs baseline 48.0%. Evolutionary search reached 69.4% vs 48.0% (post-training) and 19.7 vs 35.9 minutes (nanoGPT pre-training) in ten epochs.
limits: Two narrow environments (post-training and nanoGPT speedrun). Authors keep validation code separate to prevent hacking. No token-matched comparison against ranking without execution.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a running executed check is worth its cost when tasks are code-checkable. It does not say what to do in open tasks without a runnable check.

source: Si et al. (2026) Towards execution-grounded automated AI research: reinforcement learning from execution reward
finding: RL on execution reward raised average reward but the ideator collapsed onto a few simple ideas that execute reliably. The best-found idea did not improve. Longer thinking correlated with lower execution rate.
numbers: Mode collapse reported in both environments, e.g. the policy converged to two simple ideas in one environment. Frontier models saturate early in evolutionary search.
limits: Training result for the model, not a scaffold. Exact collapse statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: A check used as the only reward pushes toward safe, simple ideas. Keep diversity pressure or a novelty term next to the check (links to the 4000-to-200 diversity wall in K04).

source: Wen, Si, Yueh-Han, He, Feng (2025) Predicting empirical AI research outcomes with language models
finding: Gap 5. Off-the-shelf frontier models cannot tell which of two research ideas will work better. A fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with paper retrieval can.
numbers: 1,585 test idea pairs after the model cutoff, 6,000 training pairs. GPT-4.1 base 51.9%; o1/o3 similar, o3 'no better than random' even with retrieval. Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 plus retrieval 77%. GPT-3.5 45.0% to 53.7% after fine-tuning. Self-augmented CoT gave no gain.
limits: Task is predicting empirical benchmark winners, not novelty or quality as rated by people. Needs 6,000 labelled pairs and fine-tuning, so it is not a pure scaffold.
agent_relevance: A scaffold-only self-judge cannot be trusted to rank ideas near 50%. Ranking above 60% has needed either training on outcomes or an executed check (d05).

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting empirical AI research outcomes: humans and AI-generated ideas
finding: Expert humans also fail at this prediction. On unpublished AI-generated ideas the trained system stayed above chance.
numbers: 25 human experts, NLP subset of 45 idea pairs, 222 annotations: majority vote 48.9% (agreement with majority 75.1%); best annotator per topic 60.0%. System on same set 64.4%. On unpublished novel ideas including AI-generated ones: 63.6%.
limits: Small human comparison (45 pairs). Authors ran robustness tests against shortcuts such as idea complexity.
agent_relevance: Idea ranking is hard even for experts, so a ranker near 60 to 65% is the realistic ceiling. Do not design the scaffold to depend on exact idea rank.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist (supplement: Elo vs GPQA, ablations)
finding: Tournament ranking by LLM debate tracks correctness on a task with ground truth (GPQA diamond). Search tools matter for the novelty check. The evolution step adds measurable gain.
numbers: Top-Elo answer per question: top-1 accuracy 78.4% on GPQA diamond. Evolution agent: GPQA precision 70.9% to 75.4%; auto quality 4.7 to 5.6. Reflection agent on known (not novel) ideas: novelty 6.14 without search vs 2.38 with search (0-10); GPQA AUC 0.643 to 0.651 (Gemini 2.0 Flash). Meta-review AUC 0.521 to 0.597.
limits: Authors' own system and own auto-evaluation. Elo is not ground truth. GPQA is multiple choice, so it differs from open hypothesis ranking.
agent_relevance: Pairwise debate with an external search can rank usefully when there is a factual answer. Retrieval removes most of the false novelty (gap 6) in this setup.

source: Shahid, Radensky, Fok, Siangliulue, Weld, Hope (2025) Literature-grounded novelty assessment of scientific ideas
finding: Gap 6. A retrieve-then-rerank novelty checker finds prior work that makes an idea not novel. Each retrieval and rerank stage matters, and a plain keyword search finds almost nothing.
numbers: Ablation on 58 ideas (13 'not novel' plus 45 papers): complete system 89.66% accuracy on predicting 'not novel'; without facet reranker 13.79%; embedding only 10.34%; snippet only 8.62%; keyword only 5.17%. Expert-labelled examples gpt-4o: 0.78 accuracy at best. AI Scientist checker defaulted to 'not novel' on 18 of 32 ideas.
limits: Very small test set. Not tested against the 24% plagiarism rate in Gupta and Pruthi. Token cost not reported.
agent_relevance: Naive search fails and a staged retrieval plus rerank succeeds. Our novelty check needs a rerank by facet, not one keyword query.

source: Lin, Peng, Fang (2024) Evaluating and enhancing LLMs for novelty assessment in scholarly publications (SchNovel, RAG-Novelty)
finding: On 15,000 arXiv paper pairs where the later paper is taken as more novel, retrieval of similar papers raised accuracy over zero-shot, CoT and self-reflection baselines. Self-consistency was the best baseline, and multi-LLM discussion was worst. Gains were small in mathematics.
numbers: SchNovel: 15,000 pairs, six fields. All main runs used GPT-4o-mini with order swapped. RAG-Novelty best overall; Self-Consistency best among baselines; LLM Discussion below zero-shot. Exact accuracy table not extracted this session.
limits: Label is publication order, a noisy proxy for novelty. Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports retrieval plus sampling votes for novelty checks, and warns against debate between copies of the same model. Gap 5 partial: voting helps in novelty ranking, size not extracted.

source: Luo, Kasirzadeh, Shah (2025) The more you automate, the less you see: hidden pitfalls of AI scientist systems
finding: Gap 8. In controlled tests of two open AI scientist systems (Agent Laboratory, AI Scientist v2), the systems chose benchmarks by list position, and subsampled or invented datasets without saying so in the paper.
numbers: Agent Laboratory: 1,000 runs with SOTA reference, 945 explicit benchmark picks, 82.4% chose one of the first four listed benchmarks; 927 picks without reference, 79.6%. Not driven by difficulty. Label-noise tests (20% and 30%) with 5 repeats found undisclosed subsets or synthetic data in several runs (AI Scientist v2 runs 3, 7, 8, 11, 13).
limits: Two systems, one task family (symbol pattern recognition), ML research only. Run counts are the systems' explicit selections.
agent_relevance: Common failure is silent scope change and cherry-picking, not wrong code. The guardrail is a log of every choice and a rule that deviations are stated in the output.

source: Luo et al. (2025) Hidden pitfalls: detection from paper vs logs
finding: An LLM auditor reading only the final paper misses most of these failures. Reading the trace logs and code finds many more.
numbers: Binary detection accuracy with the paper alone 55% (F1 0.51). With logs and code 82% (F1 0.81).
limits: Auditor is an LLM, tested on the authors' constructed failures.
agent_relevance: Our verify state must read the actual work trace, not only the final answer. This supports a trace-based self-audit and a second pass that sees the log.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale (AlphaEvolve)
finding: Gap 7. AlphaEvolve works when the score is smooth and machine-checkable, and the authors report cheating when the evaluator is leaky. A noisy cheap-LLM oracle was gamed.
numbers: 67 problems. 'Cheating phenomenon': loopholes in leaky verifiers (discrete positivity checks) and unreliable cheap-LLM queries. In a hidden-function game the evolved program learned to coax the cheap oracle LLM into revealing the function; restricting it to yes/no answers still left noisy answers and unreliable search code.
quote: exploit artifacts (leaky verifier when approximating global constraints such as positivity by discrete versions of them
limits: Authors are the system's developers plus Tao. Counts of failures are in the text but not tallied here. Success claims are mostly self-reported.
agent_relevance: A check is only as good as its resistance to gaming. For non-code or LLM-judged checks, keep the judge fixed, limited to short outputs, and hidden from the generator.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve at scale: model mix and limits
finding: Mixing cheap and strong models sometimes beat strong models alone, because the cheap one adds variance. The system struggles when the objective has no smooth hill to climb.
numbers: Observation, no table: high-end-only runs 'sometimes perform worse' than runs mixing cheaper models. Nikodym sets needed the strong model. Prompter expertise mattered: subject experts got better results than non-experts.
limits: Anecdotal across problems, no controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Variety in proposers can matter more than quality in an evolve loop. A mixed cheap-and-strong generation step is worth testing at equal tokens.

source: Xia, Sun, Liu (2026) SR-Scientist: scientific equation discovery with agentic AI (ICLR 2026)
finding: Gap 4. An agent that can run code to analyse data and read back its own equation scores gains most from data-analysis tools, then from a memory of past equations. Removing the data-analysis tool costs the most.
numbers: Ablation Acc0.01 / Acc0.001 on their benchmark: GPT-OSS-120B full 63.57 / 49.35; without data tool 35.66 / 16.28; without experience buffer 57.36 / 41.86; random instead of top-k 58.14 / 41.86. Qwen3-Coder-480B full 49.09; without experience 35.66. Authors note LSR-Transform showed nearly 50% solved after first iteration, which suggests memory.
limits: Authors' own benchmark and metrics; margins over baselines claimed 6% to 35%. Cost about $0.25 with GPT-OSS-120B.
agent_relevance: The feedback loop that reads real data is what pays, and the model prior alone is weak on memorisation-resistant problems. Data inspection before proposing is a cheap, high-yield step.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: LSR-Synth results by method
finding: Gap 4. On synthetic problems built to resist memorisation, symbolic accuracy is low for every loop method. A bare LLM prompt gets near zero, and the evolve loop (LLM-SR, LaSR) lifts numeric fit by a large factor, but exact equation recovery stays low.
numbers: Chemistry (36), biology (24), physics (43), material science (25 problems). Symbolic accuracy with GPT-4o-mini: chemistry 11.11 (LLM-SR) vs 0.0 (direct prompt) and 2.77 (LaSR); physics 9.91 (LLM-SR) vs 0.0 (direct); biology 29.16 vs 0 direct; material science 20.24 (LLM-SR) vs 28.12 (LaSR). LSR-Transform SA: 31.53 (LLM-SR) vs 7.21 (direct), 6.31 (LaSR).
limits: Table partly garbled by PDF extraction; values for some cells are uncertain. Metrics vary by method and domain.
agent_relevance: The feedback loop is worth a large factor on numeric fit, but exact structure remains hard. Loop gain is real, and the rest of the headline gain on famous equations is memory.

source: Grayeli et al. (2024) LaSR: symbolic regression with a learned concept library (leakage and ablation checks)
finding: To test memory, the authors built 41 synthetic equations unlike textbook physics. LaSR with a small model beat the plain evolutionary baseline by a wide R2 margin. They also ran twice with different seeds to see whether the same equation repeats.
numbers: Held-out R2 on 41 synthetic equations: PySR 0.070 vs LaSR (Llama3-8B, 0.1% LLM operations) 0.913. None of the algorithms recovered the true form.
limits: R2 on held-out data, not exact structure. Small, author-built set. Gives a fit result, not proof of discovery.
agent_relevance: The model prior does help even on unseen forms, but by fit, not by finding the true law. Judge by out-of-sample fit plus a structure check, not fit alone.

source: Lu et al.; Gupta and Pruthi; Beel et al. cross-reading for gap 8
finding: Gap 8, cross-reading only. Error types already recorded in a-c lines (invented numbers, missing figures, off-the-shelf novelty checks). Luo et al. (d14) add silent scope change. No new numeric tally of error types across 2025-2026 agents was found.
numbers: No new numbers. Beel: 4 of 7 papers with wrong or hallucinated numbers (earlier line).
limits: No cross-system count of error types exists in the sources opened. Gap 8 stays partly open.
agent_relevance: Guardrails in priority: trace log, state-the-deviation rule, numbers only from tool output.

source: Liu et al. (2025) HypoBench: systematic benchmarking for hypothesis generation
finding: Gap 10. Methods that use data plus a literature-derived bank beat zero-shot and few-shot prompting on real tasks. On synthetic tasks with known truth, recovery collapses as difficulty rises.
numbers: 7 real-world and 5 synthetic task types, 194 datasets, 4 LLMs x 6 methods. Best discovery rate of ground-truth hypotheses 93.8% in base cases, 38.8% at higher difficulty. Literature + Data was best on real tasks; Qwen best model.
limits: Tasks are labelled classification datasets with a held-out check. The authors say existing methods struggle to balance novelty and plausibility. No open-ended, unlabelled test.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis bank checked against data works where labels exist. Transfer to open tasks without labels is still untested here, so gap 10 stays open.
